title: Kahana vs Udemy: Enroll There, Discuss Here
excerpt: Udemy is large course marketplace, search, ratings, and enrollment at scale for instructors who want marketplace distribution. Kahana is discovery + cohort discussion around teaching you already run elsewhere.

columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: 2025: USD 796M LTM revenue in the first three quarters; consumer ≈USD 389.8M and business ≈USD 206M as of Q3 2025.
Two segments: Consumer (individual course buyers) and Udemy Business (corporate/enterprise training).

strengths.title: Huge variety of courses
strengths.detail: 250k+ courses across programming, data science, business, design, personal development, and more.

strengths.title: Affordable pricing and frequent discounts
strengths.detail: Deep sales are common; many courses cost far less than traditional education or premium platforms.

strengths.title: Lifetime access to purchases
strengths.detail: Purchased courses typically stay available for ongoing self-paced review.

strengths.title: Strong review system and social proof
strengths.detail: Thousands of ratings and reviews help learners choose by instructor reputation and feedback.

weaknesses.title: Highly variable course quality
weaknesses.detail: Marketplace model means excellent and mediocre courses sit side by side; instructor expertise and teaching style vary widely.

weaknesses.title: Course discovery overwhelm
weaknesses.detail: Sheer volume makes finding the best option hard; learners lean heavily on ratings and external recommendations.

weaknesses.title: Low perceived credential value
weaknesses.detail: Strong for skill acquisition, but certificates are often not treated as equal to accredited or more selective platforms.

weaknesses.title: “Course hoarding” behavior
weaknesses.detail: Frequent sales encourage buying many courses that never get finished, binge purchasing over completion.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Udemy is large course marketplace, search, ratings, and enrollment at scale for instructors who want marketplace distribution. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Udemy is an online learning and teaching marketplace with over 250,000 courses and 80 million students.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Udemy side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Udemy you can use Courses, Memberships, Community & Messaging, and Marketplaces as first-class product jobs. You are running a full course engine: drip, quizzes, student progress, and checkout that already works.

Using Kahana with Udemy

You can use both. Udemy keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep the course engine on Udemy for drip, quizzes, and enrollment. Also list or link that teaching on Kahana so Explore, Clubs, and Aura can give it another place to be found. Udemy stays the LMS; Kahana is another surface for exposure.
